blocks.text: Singular value decomposition, almost always shortened to SVD, breaks any matrix at all, square or rectangular, invertible or not, into three simpler pieces: a rotation, a stretch along fixed axes, and another rotation. It is one of the most broadly useful tools in all of linear algebra, sitting underneath compression, recommendation systems, and PCA alike.

blocks.caption: The three pieces SVD splits a matrix into, and where they lead

blocks.text: 1. What SVD Decomposes a Matrix Into

SVD writes any matrix A as the product of three matrices, A = U Sigma V^T. U and V are both orthogonal matrices, as covered in the orthogonality lesson, made of orthonormal columns, and Sigma is a diagonal matrix, similar in shape to the identity matrix, but with non negative numbers called singular values along its diagonal instead of all 1s.

code.content:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[3, 0], [4, 5]])
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
print(U.shape, S.shape, Vt.shape)   # (2,2) (2,) (2,2)

blocks.text: Every matrix has an SVD, without exception, which already sets it apart from eigenvalue decomposition, which only cleanly applies to square matrices, and only some of those.

The name singular value comes from the fact that these numbers reveal how singular, meaning how close to non-invertible, a matrix is: a singular value near zero signals a direction the matrix nearly collapses entirely, echoing the singular matrix terminology from the matrix inverse lesson.
2. What Each Piece Means Geometrically

Reading the formula right to left tells the geometric story. V transposed rotates the input space into a convenient orientation. Sigma then stretches or shrinks along each of those new axes by its corresponding singular value. U rotates the result once more into its final orientation. Every linear transformation, no matter how complicated it looks, is secretly just rotate, stretch, rotate.

blocks.alt: SVD turns a circle into an ellipse
blocks.caption: Sigma stretches unevenly along two perpendicular axes, U and V orient that ellipse

blocks.text: This picture, a circle turning into a rotated, stretched ellipse, is the standard way to visualize what any matrix does to space, and it is exactly what the three SVD pieces capture individually.

Rotations never change lengths or angles, only Sigma is responsible for any actual stretching or shrinking, which is exactly why the singular values sitting on its diagonal fully capture how much a matrix distorts space, independent of orientation.
3. Singular Values and Eigenvalues

Singular values are closely related to, but not identical to, eigenvalues. Specifically, the singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A transposed A, a matrix that is always symmetric, connecting directly to the eigenvalues lesson guarantee that symmetric matrices have clean, real, non-negative eigenvalues to take a square root of.

code.content:
A = np.array([[3, 0], [4, 5]])
ATA = A.T.dot(A)
eigenvalues, _ = np.linalg.eig(ATA)
print(np.sqrt(np.sort(eigenvalues)[::-1]))   # matches the singular values from np.linalg.svd(A)

blocks.text: For a symmetric matrix specifically, the singular values and the absolute values of the eigenvalues turn out to be exactly the same numbers, but for a general, non-symmetric or non-square matrix, only singular values are guaranteed to exist and behave well.

Taking a square root is always safe here specifically because A transposed A is guaranteed symmetric, and additionally guaranteed to have non-negative eigenvalues, so there is never a negative number under the square root to worry about.
4. SVD in Code

Numpy singular values come back already sorted from largest to smallest, and reconstructing the original matrix from the three pieces confirms the decomposition is exact, aside from tiny floating point rounding.

code.content:
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
Sigma = np.zeros_like(A, dtype=float)
np.fill_diagonal(Sigma, S)
reconstructed = U.dot(Sigma).dot(Vt)
print(np.allclose(A, reconstructed))   # True

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: For a 2 by 2 matrix, Sigma has only 2 diagonal entries to fill in, but for a taller or wider rectangular matrix, Sigma is only square along its shorter dimension, with the remaining rows or columns padded with zeros, exactly matching the shape needed to multiply U, Sigma, and V transposed back together correctly.

blocks.text: 5. SVD Always Exists, Even for Rectangular Matrices

Eigenvalue decomposition, covered in the eigenvalues and eigenvectors lessons, only applies to square matrices. SVD has no such restriction, it works identically well on a 3 by 7 matrix, a 500 by 2 matrix, or anything else, which is why SVD, rather than eigen decomposition, is the tool of choice whenever the matrix in question is not guaranteed to be square.

code.content:
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])   # a 2 by 3, non-square matrix
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(B)
print(U.shape, S.shape, Vt.shape)   # (2,2) (2,) (3,3), still works fine

blocks.text: This is a large part of why SVD, rather than eigenvalue decomposition, is the default choice whenever the shape of the matrix in question is not known in advance to be square, such as a features by samples data matrix that rarely has equal rows and columns.
6. SVD and Rank

The number of nonzero singular values a matrix has is exactly its rank, as covered in the rank of matrix lesson. A matrix with 2 nonzero singular values and 1 that is effectively zero has rank 2, regardless of its overall size.

code.content:
M = np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])   # the familiar rank-1 example from earlier lessons
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M)
print(S)   # something like [5. 0.], one singular value is 0
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(M))   # 1, matching the single nonzero singular value

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: This gives yet another way to test for rank deficiency, in addition to the determinant and eigenvalue based tests covered in the rank of matrix and eigenvalues lessons: count the singular values that are meaningfully above zero, using the same numerical tolerance idea covered in the rank of matrix lesson.

blocks.text: This rank reading is one reason SVD is often the tool reached for when rank needs to be computed reliably on real, floating point data, since numpy matrix_rank itself is implemented internally using exactly this singular value threshold approach.
7. Low Rank Approximation via SVD

The rank of matrix lesson introduced low rank approximation as replacing a matrix with the closest matrix of a smaller, chosen rank. SVD is exactly the tool that makes this possible, and it is provably the best possible answer: keeping only the top k singular values and their matching U and V columns gives the single closest rank-k matrix to the original, a guarantee known as the Eckart-Young theorem.

code.content:
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
k = 1
A_rank1 = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]   # the best possible rank-1 approximation of A

blocks.text: This guarantee holds under a specific, standard measure of matrix closeness, which is enough for essentially every practical purpose, image compression, denoising, or reducing a dataset, where the goal is simply to preserve as much of the original signal as possible for a given storage budget.
7.1 Why Keeping the Largest Singular Values Is Optimal

Each singular value measures how much of the original matrix behavior that particular rotate-stretch-rotate direction accounts for. Dropping the smallest singular values first, rather than any other subset, throws away the least important behavior possible, which is precisely why this greedy approach happens to also be mathematically optimal.
8. SVD and PCA

The eigenvalues lesson previewed PCA as ranking directions in a dataset by variance using the eigenvalues of a covariance matrix. SVD applied directly to a centered data matrix, rather than to its covariance matrix, produces the exact same principal directions, and is in fact the numerically preferred way most real PCA implementations actually compute their answer.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Running SVD on a centered dataset matrix X gives singular values that are directly proportional to the standard deviations along each principal direction, and the V matrix columns are exactly the principal component directions PCA reports. The PCA intuition lesson immediately ahead in this module walks through this relationship in full.

blocks.text: Computing PCA via SVD directly on the data, rather than first building a separate covariance matrix, avoids a numerical precision loss that can occur when squaring values to form the covariance matrix, which is why most production grade PCA implementations default to the SVD route.
9. SVD for Compression

An image can be treated as a large matrix of pixel intensities, and applying the low rank approximation from section 7 to that matrix compresses the image by keeping only its most significant singular values, discarding fine detail that contributes little to the overall picture.

code.content:
# conceptual: img is a large matrix of pixel values
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(img)
k = 20   # keep only the top 20 singular values out of possibly hundreds
compressed = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]   # far smaller to store, close to the original visually

blocks.text: This same compression logic, keep the largest few singular values, discard the rest, applies identically to any large matrix, not just images, including recommendation matrices and word co-occurrence matrices used in classical natural language processing.

The compression ratio achieved this way depends entirely on how quickly the singular values fall off, images with large smooth regions compress dramatically well under SVD, while images packed with fine, random detail compress far less, since many singular values are needed to capture that detail.
10. SVD and the Pseudo-Inverse

The matrix inverse lesson introduced the pseudo-inverse as a way to invert a matrix that has no ordinary inverse, such as a non-square or singular matrix. SVD gives the cleanest possible way to compute it directly: invert each nonzero singular value, transpose the pieces, and multiply back together.

code.content:
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
S_inv = np.diag([1/s if s > 1e-10 else 0 for s in S])   # invert only the meaningfully nonzero singular values
pseudo_inverse = Vt.T.dot(S_inv).dot(U.T)
print(np.allclose(pseudo_inverse, np.linalg.pinv(A)))   # True

blocks.text: Zeroing out the reciprocal of any near-zero singular value, rather than dividing by it directly, is precisely what keeps the pseudo-inverse numerically stable, a direct callback to the numerical rank tolerance caveat covered in the rank of matrix lesson.
11. SVD in Recommendation Systems

A classic recommendation system approach represents users and items as a large, mostly empty ratings matrix, then applies a low rank SVD to discover a small number of hidden, latent factors, like genre preference or price sensitivity, that explain most of the observed ratings. Multiplying the reduced U, Sigma, and V pieces back together fills in predicted ratings for items a user has not rated yet.

items: The rank chosen for the approximation controls how many latent factors the model is allowed to use, fewer factors generalize better on sparse data, more factors capture finer grained preferences.
This is the same low rank approximation idea from section 7, applied to a ratings matrix instead of an image.

blocks.text: Real production recommendation systems rarely run plain SVD directly on the raw ratings matrix, since most entries are missing rather than zero, but the underlying intuition, factor a large sparse matrix into a small number of latent directions, traces directly back to the SVD idea covered in this lesson.
12. Explained Variance and Choosing k

Choosing how many singular values to keep in a low rank approximation, the k from section 7, is rarely arbitrary in practice. A common approach is to compute how much of the total squared singular value sum the top k values already account for, called explained variance, and stop once that fraction crosses a chosen threshold, such as 95 percent.

code.content:
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
total = np.sum(S ** 2)
explained = np.cumsum(S ** 2) / total
k = np.searchsorted(explained, 0.95) + 1   # smallest k that explains at least 95 percent

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: If the first 2 singular values out of 10 already account for 96 percent of the total squared singular value sum, keeping just those 2 gives a rank-2 approximation that captures nearly all of the original matrix behavior, while discarding 8 dimensions worth of storage and compute.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Decompose the matrix [[4, 0], [3, 5]] and confirm the singular values match the square roots of the eigenvalues of A transposed A, following the connection from section 3.

code.content:
A = np.array([[4, 0], [3, 5]])
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
print(S)                                    # singular values, largest first
print(np.sqrt(sorted(np.linalg.eigvals(A.T.dot(A)), reverse=True)))   # should match S closely

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quantity","Result"],"rows":[["singular values","approximately 6.7 and 3.0"],["rank (nonzero singular values)","2, full rank"]]}

blocks.text: Both singular values coming out clearly above zero confirms this particular matrix is full rank, matching the same conclusion the determinant or eigenvalue based tests from the rank of matrix and eigenvalues lessons would also reach.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming SVD only works on square matrices, it is precisely the tool that removes that restriction, which is one of its main advantages over eigenvalue decomposition.
Confusing singular values with eigenvalues directly, they are only identical for symmetric matrices, in general singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A transposed A.
Forgetting that numpy returns V transposed, not V itself, using it directly as V in the reconstruction formula silently produces wrong results.
Choosing an arbitrarily large k when a low rank approximation was the entire point, defeating the purpose of the compression or noise removal the truncation was meant to provide.

blocks.text: A related trap: assuming a larger k always means a strictly better approximation is guaranteed to be more useful downstream, when in practice a smaller k that removes noisy, low-signal directions can sometimes generalize better than keeping every singular value available.
15. Practice: Reconstruct from a Truncated SVD
Take a 3 by 3 matrix of your own choosing, compute its full SVD, then reconstruct it using only the top 1 singular value, and compare visually or numerically how much information was lost.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 10]])
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A)
approx = U[:, :1] @ np.diag(S[:1]) @ Vt[:1, :]
print(np.linalg.norm(A - approx))   # how far the rank-1 approximation is from the original

items: Comparing the full reconstruction against the rank-1 approximation directly demonstrates the tradeoff from section 7 and section 9 between compression and fidelity.

blocks.text: Try repeating this same exercise with a rank-2 approximation instead of rank-1, and notice how much closer the reconstruction gets, this is the explained variance idea from section 12 made directly visible in a small, hand checkable example.
Key Takeaway

Choosing k, from section 12, is the practical decision every real use of SVD eventually comes down to, whether compressing an image, factorizing a ratings matrix, or reducing a dataset with PCA immediately ahead: keep enough singular values to preserve what matters, and no more.

SVD writes any matrix, square or not, as A = U Sigma V^T, a rotation, a stretch along fixed perpendicular axes, and another rotation. Its singular values reveal rank, its truncated form gives the mathematically best possible low rank approximation, and it always exists, unlike eigenvalue decomposition which is restricted to square matrices.

This single decomposition quietly powers the PCA intuition lesson immediately ahead, image and data compression, recommendation system factorization, and the pseudo-inverse from the matrix inverse lesson, making it one of the most broadly reused tools introduced anywhere in this module.

Because SVD works on any matrix without exception, it is often the safer default reached for first, with eigenvalue decomposition reserved for the specific cases, square and often symmetric matrices, where it applies cleanly and offers a more direct interpretation.
